title: Hardness of integer linear feasibility with cyclic support
summary: We prove that integer linear feasibility is strongly $NP$-complete even when the constraint matrix has exactly two nonzero entries in every row and column, with its support forming a single cycle. This holds already for monotone systems (one positive and one negative coefficient in each inequality) with nonzero coefficients of absolute value $2$ or $3$ and right-hand sides in $\{-1,0,1,2\}$. No variable bounds are supplied separately from the system. For systems in which each inequality involves at most two variables, this strengthens known hardness results by restricting all numerical data to fixed finite sets. For systems in which each variable occurs in at most two inequalities, this establishes, to the best of our knowledge, the first $NP$-hardness result for feasibility. We also give negative answers, unless $P=NP$, to questions on polynomial-time solvability of integer programs with bounded coefficients and bounded totally $Δ$-modular treewidth, and on fixed-parameter tractability of integer bound propagation with respect to coefficient and right-hand-side magnitudes.

title: An order-reversing embedding of Turing degrees into Arthur-Nimue-Merlin degrees (short version)
comments: 18 pages, comments welcome. Conference version of arXiv:2603.19946, accepted at CSL 2027
summary:
The Arthur-Nimue-Merlin degrees are a generalization of the Turing degrees introduced by Kihara as a tangible description of the partially ordered set of Lawvere-Tierney topologies on the effective topos (equivalently, subtoposes of the effective topos). They are defined in terms of a three-player game that introduces both angelic and demonic non-determinism into oracle queries. We construct an order embedding of the Turing degrees with their order reversed into the Arthur-Nimue-Merlin degrees, whose image we call the "co-Turing degrees"; we then study the order relationship of these co-Turing degrees with the (naturally embedded) Turing degrees within the Arthur-Nimue-Merlin degrees.
  This is a short version of arXiv:2603.19946, focused on the main results.
comment: 18 pages, comments welcome. Conference version of arXiv:2603.19946, accepted at CSL 2027

title: Unifying Central Flow, Rod Flow, and the Edge Coupling
summary: At the edge of stability, the iterates of gradient descent oscillate along the sharp directions of the Hessian. This poses a significant challenge for continuous-time models as the usual continuous-time approximation -- the gradient flow -- admits no oscillations. Several continuous-time models have been proposed to capture the behavior at the edge of stability, among them central flow and rod flow. Although both models can be interpreted as performing a coarse-graining in time, the connection between them remains poorly understood. Here we show that both flows can be derived from a third object, the edge coupling: a functional on consecutive iterates whose critical points are the fixed points and period-two orbits of gradient descent. It is revealed that the two flows correspond to coarse-grainings at different time scales. Rod flow coarse-grains over only the fastest time scale, while central flow coarse-grains over both the fast and intermediate time scales. Furthermore, using the edge coupling, we derive rod flows and central flows for momentum methods such as heavy ball and Adam. We verify the derived flows experimentally on representative neural network architectures, where they track the discrete iterates throughout all phases of training -- including the transition from the stable regime to the edge of stability.

title: A Theoretical Analysis of a Bilevel Optimization Formulation for Combined Local-Global Optical Flow Models
comments: 31 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to the Journal of Mathematical Imaging and Vision. Python code in the ancillary files
summary: This paper analyzes a bilevel formulation for learning the regularization parameter of combined local-global (CLG) optical flow models. The lower-level problem computes the flow from a Lucas--Kanade data term and a quadratic or total variation (TV) regularizer, and the upper-level problem selects the parameter that minimizes the squared distance to a ground-truth flow. The setting is finite-dimensional, and a full-rank assumption makes the lower-level solution unique. For the quadratic model we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of an optimal parameter, for every optimal parameter to be positive, and for strict local optimality. For TV regularization an optimal parameter always exists, because the lower-level solution vanishes for large parameters, and we give a sufficient condition for positivity that accounts for the coupling of the two flow components through the local structure tensors. Synthetic examples illustrate the conditions, including cases in which they fail.
comment: 31 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to the Journal of Mathematical Imaging and Vision. Python code in the ancillary files

title: Polynomial-time classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss
summary: Sampling experiments are a leading approach to demonstrating quantum computational advantage, yet their robustness to experimental noise is not completely understood. We develop a common framework for classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss, including pure loss. For Fock-state boson sampling, Gaussian boson sampling with fixed uniform squeezing, and fermion sampling with magic inputs, we obtain polynomial-time sampling at inverse-polynomial total variation error, for any fixed nonzero overall loss rate, and with high probability over Haar-random interferometers. A milder flatness assumption on the ideal output distribution suffices for quasipolynomial-time simulation without Haar randomness. With constant thermal loss per layer, the same flatness assumption gives polynomial-time simulation at logarithmic depth. Our bounds for Fock-state boson sampling cover both dilute and saturated regimes and become stronger near full input filling: when only a bounded number of input modes are empty, the noisy output for Haar-random interferometers converges, as the number of modes grows, to a distribution independent of the interferometer.

title: Tusnády's problem and online two-sample thinning
summary:
We determine the sharp order of discrepancy in Tusnády's problem in every fixed dimension $d\ge 2$. The largest combinatorial discrepancy of $N$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with respect to axis-parallel boxes is $Θ_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$, extending Wei's planar result and matching Nikolov's upper bound. More strongly, with high probability, this lower bound holds simultaneously for every subset obtained by deleting at most a sufficiently small fixed fraction of a uniform $N$-point sample.
  We apply this geometric estimate to online thinning of two independent samples of size $n$ from an unknown common distribution, where observations must be kept or discarded upon arrival. For every fixed dimension $k\ge 1$ and expected deletion budget $ρn$, with $0<ρ<2$, we prove that the minimax expected prefix discrepancy over lower orthants is $Θ_{k,ρ}((\log n)^{k+1/2})$. In dimension one, the optimal terminal discrepancy is instead $Θ_ρ((\log\log n)^{3/2})$, giving a sharp separation between the prefix and terminal objectives. For $k\ge 2$, we obtain terminal bounds differing by a factor of $\log n$.
  The lower bounds are based on Gaussian small-ball estimates for box-incidence matrices, while the upper bounds use stationary Metropolis thinning and, in one dimension, a terminal cancellation procedure.

title: Parameterized Complexity of Fair Vertex Evaluation Problems
summary:
Graph modification problems form a unifying framework for many classical graph problems, where the goal is to remove a minimum number of vertices so that the resulting graph satisfies a desired property $π$. In this work, we replace the classical objective of minimizing the solution size with the fair objective [Lin&Sahni: Fair edge deletion problems. IEEE Trans. Comput. 89], which minimizes the maximum number of deleted neighbors incident to any vertex. This fairness criterion aims to distribute deletions evenly across the graph and leads to new algorithmic and complexity challenges.
  We study fair deletion and evaluation problems in the logical setting, where the target property~$π$ is defined by a formula in a logic $\mathsf{L}$. In particular, we consider the Fair $\mathsf{L}$ Vertex Evaluation problem, which asks whether there exists a vertex set $W$ of bounded fair cost such that a given formula $\varphi(X)$ holds in the input graph $G$.
  Our main result is an FPT algorithm for the Fair MSO$_1$ Vertex Evaluation problem with one free variable, parameterized by the twin cover number of the input graph and the quantifier length of the formula. We further show that extending this result to formulas with $\ell$ free variables is unlikely: the $\ell$-Fair FO Vertex Evaluation problem is W[1]-hard for parameter $\ell$ even on graphs of twin cover one. As a concrete case study, we investigate the Fair Vertex Cover}\ problem, one of the simplest fairness-aware graph problems. We prove that it is W[1]-hard when parameterized by the combined treedepth and feedback vertex set, but admits an FPT algorithm for the parameter modular width.

title: Studying word order through iterative shuffling
summary: As neural language models approach human performance on NLP benchmark tasks, their advances are widely seen as evidence of an increasingly complex understanding of syntax. This view rests upon a hypothesis that has not yet been empirically tested: that word order encodes meaning essential to performing these tasks. We refute this hypothesis in many cases: in the GLUE suite and in various genres of English text, the words in a sentence or phrase can rarely be permuted to form a phrase carrying substantially different information. Our surprising result relies on inference by iterative shuffling (IBIS), a novel, efficient procedure that finds the ordering of a bag of words having the highest likelihood under a fixed language model. IBIS can use any black-box model without additional training and is superior to existing word ordering algorithms. Coalescing our findings, we discuss how shuffling inference procedures such as IBIS can benefit language modeling and constrained generation.

title: faulTPM: Exposing AMD fTPMs' Deepest Secrets
comments: The first two authors contributed equally. We publish all code necessary to mount the attack under https://github.com/PSPReverse/ftpm_attack. The repository further includes several intermediate results, e.g., flash memory dumps, to retrace the attack process without possessing the target boards and required hardware tools
summary: Trusted Platform Modules constitute an integral building block of modern security features. Moreover, as Windows 11 made a TPM 2.0 mandatory, they are subject to an ever-increasing academic challenge. While discrete TPMs - as found in higher-end systems - have been susceptible to attacks on their exposed communication interface, more common firmware TPMs (fTPMs) are immune to this attack vector as they do not communicate with the CPU via an exposed bus. In this paper, we analyze a new class of attacks against fTPMs: Attacking their Trusted Execution Environment can lead to a full TPM state compromise. We experimentally verify this attack by compromising the AMD Secure Processor, which constitutes the TEE for AMD's fTPMs. In contrast to previous dTPM sniffing attacks, this vulnerability exposes the complete internal TPM state of the fTPM. It allows us to extract any cryptographic material stored or sealed by the fTPM regardless of authentication mechanisms such as Platform Configuration Register validation or passphrases with anti-hammering protection. First, we demonstrate the impact of our findings by - to the best of our knowledge - enabling the first attack against Full Disk Encryption solutions backed by an fTPM. Furthermore, we lay out how any application relying solely on the security properties of the TPM - like Bitlocker's TPM- only protector - can be defeated by an attacker with 2-3 hours of physical access to the target device. Lastly, we analyze the impact of our attack on FDE solutions protected by a TPM and PIN strategy. While a naive implementation also leaves the disk completely unprotected, we find that BitLocker's FDE implementation withholds some protection depending on the complexity of the used PIN. Our results show that when an fTPM's internal state is compromised, a TPM and PIN strategy for FDE is less secure than TPM-less protection with a reasonable passphrase.
